name: Chore Chart by Age
description: Age-appropriate chores from toddler to teen, plus a weekly rotation for the household jobs everyone shares.

items.text: Put toys into a basket or bin after playing
items.note: At this age the point is the habit, not the result. Expect to do it alongside them for months.

items.text: Carry their own plastic plate or cup to the sink
Put dirty clothes into the laundry basket
Fill a pet's dry food bowl using a pre-measured scoop
items.note: An adult measures; the child pours. Keep them away from water bowls that get carried.

items.text: Wipe up their own spills with a cloth
Put books back on a low shelf
Make their own bed, loosely
items.note: Pulling the duvet flat counts. Re-making it to adult standard teaches them it was never really their job.

items.text: Set the table with napkins, cutlery and unbreakable cups
Match clean socks into pairs
Water indoor plants with a small jug
Clear their own place at the table
Sort recycling into the right bin
Dust low surfaces and skirting boards with a dry cloth
Pack their own school bag the night before
items.note: Keep a short list taped inside the bag for the first few weeks.

items.text: Fold and put away their own clean laundry
Load and unload the dishwasher, skipping knives
Wipe down the bathroom sink and mirror
Sweep floors and use a dustpan
Feed and water pets without reminders
Take the bins out to the kerb on collection day
Tidy their bedroom floor before bed
Run a full load of laundry from sorting to folding
items.note: Show them the machine once with the detergent already measured, then let them run it alone.

items.text: Vacuum a whole room including under furniture edges
Prepare a simple cold meal or packed lunch
Clean the toilet with an age-safe bathroom cleaner
items.note: Check the label and keep bleach-based products out of this age band.

items.text: Change their own bed linen
Rake leaves, weed a bed, or water the garden
Help write the week's grocery list from what is missing
Wash and dry dishes by hand
Cook one family dinner a week from start to clean-up
items.note: Fixing the night in advance stops this quietly becoming optional.

items.text: Mow the lawn or clear snow from paths
Do the full grocery shop from a written list
Clean a bathroom end to end, including the floor
Mind younger siblings for a set, agreed period
Wash the car inside and out
Manage their own schedule, deadlines and appointments
Iron their own clothes
Take responsibility for one recurring household job of their choosing
items.note: Letting them pick it is what turns a chore into a contribution.

items.text: Kitchen deep clean: hob, microwave, fridge shelves
Bathrooms: toilets, showers, mirrors, floors
Floors: vacuum and mop every room
Laundry: wash, dry, fold, put away
Bins and recycling out
Change all bed linen
Grocery shop and restock staples
Tidy shared living areas before the week starts
Agree the list together before anything goes on the wall
items.note: A chart written by one person and handed down is the one that gets ignored.

items.text: Give each person no more than three daily chores
Fix a time of day for daily chores, such as before screens or after dinner
Put the chart where it is seen without being fetched
Decide in advance what happens when a chore is skipped
Decide whether chores are paid, and keep that answer consistent
Re-cut the list every school year as ages and schedules change

faq.q: What age should children start doing chores?
faq.a: Around two to three, with simple one-step jobs like putting toys in a basket or dirty clothes in the laundry. At that age the chore is not about the work getting done — it is about the child learning that the household has jobs and that they are part of it. Useful output arrives around six.

faq.q: How many chores should a child have?
faq.a: No more than about three daily chores, plus one or two weekly ones. A short list that actually happens every day beats a long list that collapses in a fortnight. Add the next chore only once the current ones no longer need reminding.

faq.q: Should children be paid for chores?
faq.a: Households split on this and both approaches work. A common middle path is to keep basic chores unpaid because they are part of living in the house, and to pay separately for larger optional jobs such as washing the car or clearing the garage. What matters most is picking one rule and not changing it when an argument starts.

faq.q: What is the difference between a chore chart and a chore list?
faq.a: A chore list is just the jobs. A chore chart adds who does each job and when, usually as a grid of names against days, so it can be checked at a glance and ticked off. The list below can be used either way: tick it as a list, or copy the names into a weekly grid.

faq.q: How do you stop having to nag about chores?
faq.a: Move the reminding onto the chart rather than onto yourself: fix a consistent time of day, put the chart somewhere visible, and agree the consequence for a skipped chore before it is skipped. The conversation then points at the chart instead of turning into a negotiation.
